But to answer the question, the trends point toward progressive demassification of production and thus expanding ownership. The factory is already an anachronism and the evolution of production points to its progressive commodification, localization, and immersion into the infrastructure. In the year 2000 our civilization passed an important but overlooked milestone. That year the volume of consumer goods produced in 'job shops'--small contract production plants mostly in Asia--surpassed the number of goods produced in traditional factories. And it never went back. Most of the stuff in our habitat is now not made by big plants owned by big corporations. The corporations only own the brands. The actual products are being made by a growing number of independent companies whose quick-adapting production capability is treated as a commodity contracted on-demand.

And there's a good reason for this. The capital overhead of production ownership is a competitive liability because it delays a company's ability to adapt to market changes. Small companies outcompete because it costs so much less in time and money for them to innovate. Owning large central production facilities mean carry large debts for decades and incurring large retooling costs to introduce new or updated products. Cars may have new models every year, but the way they are made has changed very little since the introduction of pressed-steel welded unibody construction in the 1930s. The changes of the new models are superficial--no different from altering the shape of a soda can. This is why large corporations have often taken to fighting competition through manipulation of laws and litigation rather than doing actual innovation. This is why copyright is such a major issue today.

The machines aren't just getting smarter. They're getting smaller, more versatile, and cheaper too. It's now possible to initiate many forms of production 'out of pocket' that used to require Big Capital and do it in progressively smaller facilities at progressively smaller minimum production volumes, trending toward production on-demand. More different products can be produced by the same machine with just a switch of software rather than hardware. The number of things you can't produce competitively in the space of a 2-4 car garage is slowly diminishing. Marginal costs--the cost of duplicating a product after it's developed--are rapidly falling for an increasing number of goods. The biggest portion of marginal cost is becoming capital--the cost of money.

In the Maker movement there is this undercurrent meme sometimes called 'unplugging'. It's the notion that, by leveraging the potential of new personal production tools, one can whittle-away at dependencies on the market for the things we need to live comfortably, gaining a reduction in the cost of living and a recovery in personal time and freedom. The more we can unplug from the market and make stuff for ourselves, the more of our own lives sacrificed to someone else's profit we can recover. We are some ways away from being able to realize total autarky in our own homes, but it seems tantalizingly close to those who are more 'industrially literate', and so people are actively pursuing this. However, it's not far off at the community level. The city of Barcelona recently started a project called Fab Cities to seek industrial autonomy for their city in the near future. They want everything the city needs to be produced within or nearby so they can counter the negative effects of Globalization and increase the resilience of their community in an increasingly uncertain global economy. This isn't so hard given that most of the stuff our general standard of living depends on doesn't need something like an Intel microchip plant to produce. It's already made in simple little job shops that happen to be mostly in Asia that initially exploited cheap labor but now are exploiting increasing cheap automation. But what's really interesting here is the notion of the city--its community--cultivating its own industrial infrastructure, making it a part of the urban infrastructure.

The future of production is that, through automation, it evolves to be generic, on-demand, and merges into the infrastructure of the built habitat. It becomes like the Internet. It becomes a public utility.

My kombucha developed mold the week before last and I dumped it but after doing more research I realized my mistake. I rescued the kombucha mother from my sink drain (yes, really) and washed it under the tap (chlorine, oops!). I tore off a tiny chunk and added it to a new batch of tea.

After waiting for a while I noticed cloudy lumps hanging around on the bottom of the fermenting jars. I was again concerned but, as before, research suggested that sometimes the mother sinks and everything is fine.

There were again spots of mold developing on the liquid, but I scooped them off and added two spoons of vinegar to each jar to stave off the mold until the lactic acid bacteria could further acidify the drink. Finally, with no funny smells, I noticed a new mother forming on the top of the liquid.

I poured a glass, avoiding any lumps or pieces of the mother, and tried it yesterday. It was really good! Just like a dry iced tea but with an acidic kick to it, very refreshing. It was about 10 days fermenting, which may be a bit long. It would probably be sweeter and less acidic if I drank it sooner, but I wouldn't cut the time down much.

I used a black breakfast tea brewed strong and 1/4 cup of sugar per quart of tea. I didn't notice if there were effects from the caffeine.
I ain't dead - my kombucha mother was successfully rescued from mold!
